task_title: After Landing, Parking, and Securing (ASEL, AMEL)
objective: By the end of this lesson you can clear the runway and run the after-landing flow and checklist without a slip, taxi to an unfamiliar ramp, park and shut down with people and property protected, handle fueling safely, inspect the airplane after flight, write up discrepancies the way an operator needs them, and secure the airplane for the night.
why: A commercial pilot is often the last person to touch the airplane before the next pilot, passenger or mechanic does, so what you notice and write down after landing becomes their safety margin. The FAA treats the flight as unfinished until the engine is shut down and the airplane is secured [[24:60|AFH 2-23]], and your awareness has to last until the airplane is back in its tie-down or hangar [[24:38|AFH 2-1]].

prereading.what: After-landing roll, the clear-of-runway checklist, parking, shutdown, postflight inspection, servicing and securing. Read this twice.
prereading.label: AFH 2-22 to 2-23

prereading.what: Ramp hazards, passengers, refueling, hand signals, hot magnetos and the nearly invisible propeller.
prereading.label: AFH 2-14 to 2-17

prereading.what: Why the landing is not over at touchdown: directional control, braking, ailerons and the gear-versus-flaps trap.
prereading.label: AFH 9-9 to 9-10

prereading.what: Standard taxi routes and the rules for exiting the runway after landing.
prereading.label: AIM 4-3-20 to 4-3-21

prereading.what: Single-pilot habits for the landing rollout, the exit and the taxi in, including what to leave alone until you are clear.
prereading.label: AC 91-73B pages 4 to 7

prereading.what: Fuel grades and colors, contamination, and the grounding and bonding sequence for refueling.
prereading.label: PHAK 7-27 to 7-29

prereading.what: Inspections, operating with inoperative equipment, deferrals and preventive maintenance by pilots.
prereading.label: PHAK 9-8 to 9-12

warmup: Think first: you are the third pilot to fly a rental airplane today. On the walkaround you find a fresh cut in a main tire. Nobody wrote it up. Who saw it happen, who will fix it, and who should have told them? Now picture tomorrow, when you are the pilot whose postflight decides what the next pilot inherits.

key_terms.def: All parts of the airplane are past the runway edge and nothing stops it from moving on past the runway holding position markings [[33:264|AIM 4-3-21]].
The movement area is under ATC control. Two yellow lines mark the boundary: dashed on the movement side, solid on the nonmovement side [[33:159|AIM 2-3-6c]].
A published, predictable taxi route that a pilot may request by name at some airports. Requesting one says you know it fully [[33:263|AIM 4-3-20]].
Doing the actions first, then using the checklist to confirm them. The AFH allows this as long as the checklist is really used [[24:36|AFH 1-15]].
Connecting the fuel nozzle (or drum) to the airplane so both have the same static charge before fuel flows [[1:189|PHAK 7-29]].
Connecting the airplane or fuel truck to the earth to drain static electricity. A truck is grounded before its nozzle touches the airplane [[1:189|PHAK 7-29]].
A defect the owner or operator must have repaired between required inspections [[60:520|14 CFR 91.405(a)]]. You report it in the maintenance or discrepancy record [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]].
Flying with an inoperative item without an MEL under 14 CFR 91.213(d): not required, deactivated or removed, placarded, and judged not a hazard [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)]].
Simple or minor preservation work and replacement of small standard parts, limited to the list in 14 CFR part 43, appendix A [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]].
Security Identification Display Area: a limited-access area that needs a badge issued under 49 CFR part 1542 [[33:173|AIM 2-3-15]].
Air thrown back by a running engine. It can damage and upset aircraft, vehicles and equipment at close range [[33:262|AIM 4-3-18]].

chunks.title: Same task, higher bar: the commercial view

body.p: This Task has no numbers to hold. The examiner watches whether you park with nearby people and property in mind, use the checklists, inspect the airplane after flight, document what you find, and secure the airplane (ACS CA.XI.A.S2 to S5).

The commercial ACS lists exactly the same knowledge, risk and skill elements as the private ACS (ACS PA.XII.A and CA.XI.A). What changes is the person doing it. As a commercial pilot you may act as PIC carrying persons or property for compensation or hire, when qualified for that operation [[60:322|14 CFR 61.133(a)(1)]], so other people rely on your write-ups and your judgment on the ramp.

head: Element
What the examiner looks for
rows: CA.XI.A.S2
A parking spot and heading that keep blast, people and property out of harm's way
CA.XI.A.S3
The POH after-landing, shutdown and securing checklists actually used
CA.XI.A.S4
A real walkaround, with discrepancies and servicing needs written down
CA.XI.A.S5
Chocks, tie-downs, control lock and covers as the airplane and weather need

body.p: The AFH says experienced pilots stress ground operations because safe flight begins and ends there, and hurried ground work shrinks the safety margin [[24:38|AFH 2-1]].

callout.text: The POH/AFM checklists come first. The AFH lists only typical items and tells you to use the after-landing and shutdown checklists in your airplane's AFM/POH [[24:59|AFH 2-22]] [[24:60|AFH 2-23]].

check.q: Does the commercial ACS add any new elements to this Task compared with the private ACS?
check.a: No. The elements are the same (ACS PA.XII.A and CA.XI.A). The difference is the standard of care expected of someone flying for hire.

body.p: The landing is not finished until you have slowed to normal taxi speed, or stopped clear of the landing area. Pilots who relax at touchdown lose control on the rollout [[24:180|AFH 9-9]].

bullets: Rudder controls yaw, but it weakens as you slow. Once the nosewheel is down, nosewheel steering gives more positive control [[24:180|AFH 9-9]].
Brake firmly and smoothly after the nosewheel is down. Pumping the brakes does not help, and a skid makes braking ineffective [[24:181|AFH 9-10]].
In a crosswind keep the upwind wing from rising with aileron while you steer with rudder or nosewheel steering [[24:189|AFH 9-18]].
Slow to normal taxi speed before turning off. A sharp turn at higher speed can damage the gear, tires, brakes or structure [[24:59|AFH 2-22]].

body.p: Exit rules from the AIM [[33:264|AIM 4-3-21]]:

bullets: Exit without delay at the first available taxiway, or where ATC tells you. Never exit onto another runway unless ATC authorizes it.
At a towered airport, do not stop or turn around on the runway without ATC approval.
With no other ATC instructions, taxi until every part of the airplane is past the holding position markings, even if that puts you into another taxiway or ramp. Then hold.
Switch to ground when the tower says so, and get a taxi clearance.

body.p: Traps the AC and PHAK point out [[7:7|AC 91-73B 7d(11), (12), (14)]] [[1:369|PHAK 14-35]]:

bullets: A last-minute turnoff instruction: accept it only if you clearly understand it and your speed lets you comply safely.
Exits that cross or end near another runway: use the utmost caution. If an adjacent parallel runway's hold short line keeps you from clearing your runway, stop and tell ATC right away.
Non-towered fields: not every airplane has a radio. Before entering or crossing a runway, listen on the CTAF and scan the full length plus the approach and departure paths.

callout.text: Brief the planned turnoff before landing. AC 91-73B's sample prelanding briefing includes the planned runway turnoff, the taxi route and hot spots [[7:15|AC 91-73B App 2]].

The runway boundary sign faces you as you exit and sits next to the holding position marking. It is a cue for deciding when you are clear of the runway [[33:166|AIM 2-3-9]], but the rule is about the whole airplane, tail included [[7:7|AC 91-73B 7d(11)]].

check.q: You exit at a towered airport with no further instructions. Where do you stop?
check.a: Once every part of the airplane has crossed the runway holding position markings. Then you hold until ATC gives more instructions [[33:264|AIM 4-3-21]].

body.p: Do the after-landing checklist only after a complete stop beyond the runway holding position markings, unless the manufacturer wants a specific item done on the rollout [[24:59|AFH 2-22]]. AC 91-73B says the same: change nothing until the whole airplane is past the hold short line, and start no nonessential talking or actions (frequencies, flaps, trim) until you are clear of all runways [[7:4|AC 91-73B 7b(2)(g)]] [[7:7|AC 91-73B 7d(13)]].
Typical items, to be replaced by your POH list [[24:60|AFH 2-23]]:

bullets: Power: POH value, such as 1,000 rpm, propeller full forward, mixture leaned
Fuel: switch tanks or turn fuel pumps off if required
Flaps: up
Cowl flaps: open or closed for the temperature
Trim: neutral or takeoff
Lights: off if not needed, such as strobes
Avionics: frequencies and transponder set for taxi

body.p: Commercial training usually puts you in a retractable-gear airplane. Pilots have retracted the gear instead of the flaps while still rolling. Form the habit of positively identifying both controls before you move either one [[24:181|AFH 9-10]]. In retractable airplanes, finish the landing roll and clear the runway before operating any lever or switch [[24:248|AFH 12-17]].

A flow, then the checklist. The AFH says a checklist need not be a do-list: you may do the actions and then use the checklist to confirm them, as long as you really use it. After landing and engine shutdown and securing are both on its minimum list of checklist phases [[24:36|AFH 1-15]].

head: Light
Guidance on the ground
rows: Rotating beacon
On whenever an engine is running [[7:10|AC 91-73B 7h(2)(a)]]. The AIM recommends it for commercial operators and encourages it for all [[33:266|AIM 4-3-24]]
Taxi light
Consider it on while moving, off when stopped or yielding [[33:266|AIM 4-3-24]]
Strobes
Off during taxi if they bother other pilots or ground crew [[33:266|AIM 4-3-24]]
Position lights
Required on the surface from sunset to sunrise [[33:266|AIM 4-3-24]] [[60:491|14 CFR 91.209(a)(1)]]

callout.text: Before shutdown, listen on 121.5 MHz. Hard landings are one cause of accidental ELT activation, and the AIM asks pilots to monitor before engine shutdown at the end of each flight [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4]].

check.q: On a short-field landing your POH says to raise the flaps on the rollout for better braking. What must you do first?
check.a: Positively identify the flap control before moving it [[24:59|AFH 2-22]].

chunks.title: Taxi to parking: ground, the ramp and the boundary line

body.p: Once clear and stopped, run the after-landing items, call ground, read back, look at the airport diagram and monitor your progress to parking [[7:5|AC 91-73B 7b(2)(h)]]. A taxi clearance to parking does not let you enter or cross any runway, and if you do not know the route you should ask for specific instructions [[33:264|AIM 4-3-21]].

Standard Taxi Routes: some airports publish STRs you can request by name. Asking for one tells ATC you know it fully, an STR never includes a clearance to cross a runway, and if you are unsure you should ask or decline it [[33:263|AIM 4-3-20]].

The movement area ends at the nonmovement area boundary: two yellow lines, the dashed one on the movement side and the solid one on the nonmovement side [[33:159|AIM 2-3-6c]]. Past it you are on the ramp, outside ATC control, and the people and equipment around you are your problem.
Destination signs (yellow with black lettering and an arrow) lead you to the right ramp [[33:169|AIM 2-3-11]]:

bullets: FBO Apron: itinerant parking with FBO services
GA Transient Apron: itinerant parking without FBO services
GA Tenant Apron: based aircraft, such as a tie-down area
FUEL: where aircraft get fuel or related services [[33:170|AIM 2-3-11]]

body.p: At night, check the parking ramp with a flashlight before you start; stepladders, potholes and loose chocks are hard to see in the dark [[24:225|AFH 11-8]]. Also note a night rule many pilots forget: from sunset to sunrise you may not park or move an airplane in, or dangerously close to, a night flight operations area unless it is clearly lit, has its position lights on, or sits in an area marked by obstruction lights [[60:491|14 CFR 91.209(a)(2)]].

callout.text: Expectation bias works in the taxi-in too. Follow the clearance you actually received, not the one you expected [[7:4|AC 91-73B 7b(2)(e) CAUTION]].

check.q: You taxi across a dashed yellow line and then a solid yellow line. Where are you now?
check.a: In the nonmovement area. The dashed line is on the movement (ATC) side and the solid line on the nonmovement side [[33:159|AIM 2-3-6c]].

chunks.title: Ramp safety: blast, propellers and parking

body.p: The ramp mixes airport workers, passengers, trucks, airplanes and even stray people and animals, and the pilot is responsible for operating safely among them [[24:51|AFH 2-14]]. Powerful aircraft can throw exhaust blast or rotor downwash strong enough to make a light airplane uncontrollable [[24:52|AFH 2-15]]. Prop wash, jet blast and rotor wash can damage aircraft, vehicles and equipment at close range [[33:262|AIM 4-3-18]].
Choosing the spot [[24:60|AFH 2-23]]:

bullets: Unless the area is designated and supervised, pick a spot and heading where other airplanes' prop or jet blast will not hit yours.
Head into the existing or forecast wind when you can. Tie-down rows may not line up with the wind.
After stopping in the direction you want, let the airplane roll straight ahead a little to straighten the nosewheel or tailwheel.

body.p: Your own propeller is the bigger danger to people. It is nearly invisible when turning, and people have been killed walking or reaching into it near the chocks, the cabin door or on the way to the tail [[24:54|AFH 2-17]]. A faulty magneto switch can be OFF and still let the magneto fire, so treat a stopped propeller as if the ignition were on [[24:53|AFH 2-16]].
The rotating beacon helps, but the FAA's beacon program is voluntary. Do not rely on a beacon alone to tell you whether another airplane's engine is running [[33:266|AIM 4-3-24]].

Many ramps have marshallers. The AIM shows the standard signals, including insert chocks [[33:272|AIM 4-3-26]], cut engines [[33:273|AIM 4-3-26]] and stop [[33:274|AIM 4-3-26]]. At night they use lighted wands with the same hand movements as by day [[33:273|AIM 4-3-26]], and the AFH adds that at night the emergency stop signal is used for all stops [[24:52|AFH 2-15]].

callout.text: Careless or reckless operation rules reach the ramp. You may not operate an aircraft on any part of an airport surface used for air commerce, including passenger and cargo areas, in a careless or reckless way that endangers life or property, even when you are not flying [[60:436|14 CFR 91.13(b)]].
If a marshaller signals something you do not understand or that looks unsafe, stop. The marshaller helps; you are still the pilot in command.

check.q: Why should you treat a stopped propeller as live even with the magneto switch OFF?
check.a: A faulty switch can be in the OFF position and still let the magneto fire, so the engine could start [[24:53|AFH 2-16]].

chunks.title: Shutdown: why each step is there

body.p: Always use your POH shutdown checklist. The AFH gives typical items and order [[24:60|AFH 2-23]]. The reasons column is where a commercial applicant shows understanding.

head: Typical item
Why it matters (application unless cited)
rows: Parking brake ON
Holds the airplane while you work the engine controls
Throttle IDLE or 1,000 rpm
A low, steady rpm before cutoff
Turbocharged: manufacturer's spool-down
Turbocharged engines run hotter and are especially heat sensitive [[24:242|AFH 12-11]]
Brief magneto switch check to OFF at idle
Proves the switch grounds the magnetos; a faulty switch can leave a magneto live [[24:53|AFH 2-16]]
Propeller HIGH rpm, if equipped
Per the AFH list
Avionics and alternator OFF
Per the AFH list, before the mixture
Mixture IDLE CUTOFF, then ignition OFF when the engine stops
Stops the engine by starving it of fuel
Chocks in, then release the parking brake per the POH
Holds the airplane without depending on the brake
Master OFF
Prevents a dead battery
Control locks and anti-theft locks
Protects the controls and the airplane

body.p: Item sources: [[24:60|AFH 2-23]]. The AFH lists avionics and alternator off before the mixture but does not give a reason; your POH may say why. The sources also give no spool-down time; that number is in the POH.

callout.text: Think in three blocks: Hold it (brake, idle), Prove it (mag check), Kill it (electrics off, mixture cutoff, mags off), then Keep it (chocks, master off, locks).
A flight is not complete until the engine is shut down and the airplane is secured [[24:60|AFH 2-23]]. Do not stop the checklist for a chat, a photo or a phone call.

check.q: During the mag check at idle the engine keeps running normally with the switch at OFF. What does it suggest, and what do you do?
check.a: The switch is not grounding a magneto, so the magneto could be live with the switch off [[24:53|AFH 2-16]]. Finish the shutdown with the mixture, keep everyone clear of the propeller, and write it up for maintenance.

chunks.title: Getting passengers off the airplane safely

body.p: The rules keep passengers seated until the airplane stops. Each person on board must have a safety belt (and shoulder harness, if installed) fastened during movement on the surface, takeoff and landing, and the PIC must make sure everyone has been told to fasten it [[60:441|14 CFR 91.107(a)(2), (3)]]. Ask passengers to keep a sterile cockpit from the time landing preparations begin until the airplane is safely stopped at the terminal [[7:5|AC 91-73B 7c]].
Most passengers have little ramp experience. Tell them to move only as you direct, and give them an escort if they are not under your direct supervision [[24:51|AFH 2-14]].

bullets: Brief the exit before engine start. The PHAK SAFETY briefing covers seat belts for taxi, takeoff and landing, the fire extinguisher, and how to open the exit doors [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]].
Shut down before anyone gets out. A spinning propeller can kill [[24:53|AFH 2-16]].
Keep everyone out of the propeller arc. People have walked into it on the way to the cabin or the tail [[24:54|AFH 2-17]].
Watch the ramp: other airplanes may be starting or taxiing, and their blast can throw debris into people [[24:53|AFH 2-16]].
The pilot should supervise baggage loading and security [[24:51|AFH 2-14]]; give unloading the same care (application).

callout.text: Commercial habit: say it twice. Once in the pre-start brief ('Stay seated until I open your door'), and again after shutdown ('Walk behind the wing and wait for me by the fence').

Never let passengers wander toward an airline ramp or fenced area. A SIDA needs a badge, and people seen entering without ID may be reported to TSA and face fines or prosecution [[33:174|AIM 2-3-15]].

check.q: Your passenger unbuckles while you are still taxiing to the ramp. Which rule applies?
check.a: 14 CFR 91.107(a)(3): each person must have the belt fastened during movement on the surface [[60:441|14 CFR 91.107(a)(3)]].

body.p: During refueling, take the passengers out of the airplane and watch the fueling yourself, to make sure the right fuel and quantity go in and the caps and cowls are secured afterward [[24:51|AFH 2-14]].

Know the colors. AVGAS 80 is red, 100 is green, 100LL is blue, and Jet A is colorless or straw with a kerosene smell. AVGAS equipment is marked with white letters on red; turbine fuel with white letters on black [[1:187|PHAK 7-27]]. Jet fuel trucks carry JET-A placards in white on black, and jet nozzles are flared so they will not fit an AVGAS filler [[24:45|AFH 2-8]].
Static electricity builds up from fuel flowing through the hose and nozzle, and from clothing such as nylon, Dacron or wool. Protect against a spark [[1:189|PHAK 7-29]]:

bullets: Attach a ground wire to the airplane before the fuel cap comes off.
Bond the nozzle to the airplane before fueling starts, and keep it bonded throughout.
Ground a fuel truck before its nozzle touches the airplane.
From drums: drum to ground, ground to aircraft, then drum or nozzle to aircraft before removing the cap. Disconnect in reverse order.
A chamois increases static; bond the nozzle, chamois filter and funnel to the airplane. Never use a plastic bucket or other nonconductive container.

body.p: Do not service oxygen during fueling or other work that could make a spark [[1:200|PHAK 7-40]]. After fueling, confirm the caps are back on, and check the fuel level visually: ramp slope and strut extension can change how much the tanks will hold [[24:46|AFH 2-9]].

How much to add depends on what is next. If the airplane will sit, filling the tanks limits water condensation; if another flight is planned, fuel for that flight's needs [[24:60|AFH 2-23]]. Full tanks also slow the aging of rubber tanks and sealant [[24:47|AFH 2-10]]. Plan the weight: avgas weighs 6 pounds per gallon [[22:67|W&B Handbook 7-7]].

callout.text: Commercial note: a Part 135 operator may not carry passengers unless the aircraft has approved hand fire extinguishers suited to the fires likely to occur [[6:58|14 CFR 135.155]]. Know where yours is; the SAFETY briefing tells passengers too [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]].

check.q: A fuel truck pulls up to your airplane. What must happen before its nozzle touches the airplane?

chunks.title: Postflight inspection: read the airplane while it is warm

body.p: After shutdown and deplaning, walk around the airplane [[24:60|AFH 2-23]]:

bullets: Cowling: oil or fuel streaks; the oil breather for too much oil discharge
Under the wings and other tank locations: fuel stains
Landing gear and tires: damage. Brakes: leaking hydraulic fluid
Cowling inlets: obstructions
Oil: check and bring to the POH level

body.p: Go deeper than the list. The same things the AFH tells you to check before flight are worth seeing right after one:

bullets: Propeller: erosion, nicks, cracks, pitting, corrosion and security. On a controllable-pitch (such as constant-speed) propeller, oil leaks tend to streak from the hub toward the tips [[24:49|AFH 2-12]].
Fuel stains anywhere on the wing or near a tank need a closer look, however old they seem. On wet-wing tanks look along the rivet lines [[24:46|AFH 2-9]].

Tires: inflation, tread, wear pattern, cuts, bulges, cords. On airplanes flown by several pilots, what happened to the tires earlier is unknown, so move the airplane a little to see the whole tire [[24:48|AFH 2-11]].

callout.text: Do the postflight as if it were the next pilot's preflight. Warm oil and fresh stains are easiest to trace now, and the cause is still in your memory.

check.q: You see old-looking fuel stains along the rivets under a wing. Can you ignore them?
check.a: No. Fuel stains anywhere on the wing call for further investigation no matter how old they look [[24:46|AFH 2-9]].

chunks.title: Writing up discrepancies like a professional

body.p: Who owns what:

head: Rule
What it says
rows: The PIC decides whether the aircraft is in condition for safe flight and must discontinue the flight when an unairworthy mechanical, electrical or structural condition occurs [[60:436|14 CFR 91.7]]
The owner or operator is primarily responsible for keeping the aircraft airworthy [[60:520|14 CFR 91.403(a)]]

The owner or operator has discrepancies repaired between inspections, gets deferred items fixed or inspected at the next required inspection, and makes sure placards are installed [[60:520|14 CFR 91.405(a)]] [[60:521|14 CFR 91.405(c), (d)]]

For a Part 135 operator, the PIC enters each mechanical irregularity noticed during flight time in the aircraft maintenance log, and before each flight checks the status of any irregularity entered at the end of the last flight [[6:21|14 CFR 135.65(b)]]

body.p: In-flight discrepancies are handled with the POH procedures, not with a maintenance deferral [[1:239|PHAK 9-9]]. Once you are on the ground they become your write-up.
Deferring an inoperative item without an MEL [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)]]:

bullets: It is not part of the VFR-day type certification equipment, not required by the equipment list or kinds of operations list, not required by 91.205 or another rule for the flight, and not required by an AD.
It is removed (cockpit control placarded, maintenance recorded under 43.9) or deactivated and placarded "Inoperative." If deactivation involves maintenance, it is done and recorded under part 43.
A certificated, appropriately rated pilot or maintenance person decides it is not a hazard.

body.p: Removal always counts as maintenance and must be done by certificated maintenance personnel [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]]. If an airplane has an approved MEL, its use is mandatory [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]].

Preventive maintenance by you: any part 61 pilot except a sport pilot may do preventive maintenance on an aircraft he or she owns or operates, but not on an aircraft used under part 121, 129 or 135 [[60:130|14 CFR 43.3(g)]]. The only exceptions, 43.3(h) and (i), need an FAA approval held by the Part 135 operator and cover remote-area rotorcraft items or removing and reinstalling cabin seats, stretchers and oxygen bottles [[60:130|14 CFR 43.3(h), (i)]]. The entry must describe the work, give the completion date, and carry the signature, certificate number and kind of certificate of the person approving it [[60:132|14 CFR 43.9(a)]], and that approval takes at least a private pilot certificate [[60:132|14 CFR 43.7(f)]].

callout.text: Flying for hire adds inspections. No one may carry any person (other than a crewmember) for hire, or give flight instruction for hire in an airplane he or she provides, unless the airplane has had an annual or 100-hour inspection within the preceding 100 hours of time in service. The 100 hours may be exceeded by up to 10 hours only while en route to a place where the inspection can be done, and that excess counts toward the next 100 hours [[60:521|14 CFR 91.409(b)]] [[60:522|14 CFR 91.409(b)]] [[1:238|PHAK 9-8]] [[1:239|PHAK 9-9]].

A useful squawk names the item, what it did, when, and under what conditions, plus anything you ruled out. 'Left fuel gauge reads 5 gallons low compared with dipstick, both on the ground and in cruise' gets fixed; 'fuel gauge weird' does not.

check.q: A friend who holds only a student pilot certificate co-owns a Cessna and replaces its landing light bulb himself. May he approve the airplane for return to service?
check.a: No. Approving a return to service after pilot preventive maintenance takes at least a private pilot certificate [[60:132|14 CFR 43.7(f)]], and the entry must describe the work, give the date and carry the approver's signature, certificate number and kind of certificate [[60:132|14 CFR 43.9(a)]].

chunks.title: Securing the airplane and airport security

body.p: Hangar it or tie it down, secure the flight controls, and install security locks [[24:60|AFH 2-23]].

bullets: Chains do not stretch, so do not pull them taut; leave a little movement to avoid structural damage. Ropes stretch and may be cinched reasonably to the tie-down rings [[24:60|AFH 2-23]].
Consider pitot covers, cowling inlet covers, a rudder gust lock, window sunscreens and a propeller security lock [[24:60|AFH 2-23]].
In a hangar, leave enough room so the airplane cannot hit the structure, another aircraft or a vehicle, and inspect it for damage after hangaring [[24:60|AFH 2-23]].
Chock the wheels before releasing the parking brake, as the POH directs [[24:60|AFH 2-23]].

body.p: Airport-specific security (ACS CA.XI.A.R3):

bullets: A SIDA can include parts of the movement or parking area, and a secured area (where airline passengers board) is always a SIDA. You may not go in without authorization and displayed ID [[33:173|AIM 2-3-15]].
Airports with a SIDA publish a description and boundary map; if unsure, ask the airport authority [[33:173|AIM 2-3-15]].
49 CFR 1540 requires you to show your airman or medical certificate when TSA asks [[33:174|AIM 2-3-15]].
Report suspicious activity through AOPA's Airport Watch Program, 866-427-3287 [[33:174|AIM 2-3-15]].

body.p: Escorting passengers is part of ramp security as well as safety [[24:51|AFH 2-14]].

callout.text: At a strange airport, ask the FBO three questions before you leave: the gate code or exit route, whether the ramp is part of a SIDA, and whether their tie-downs are ropes or chains.

check.q: Your tie-down spot has chains. How tight should they be?
check.a: Not taut. Leave some movement so the airframe is not damaged [[24:60|AFH 2-23]].

chunks.title: Activities and distractions at the end of the day

body.p: The end of a flight is full of activity: radio calls, a new frequency, a strange ramp, passengers eager to get out, a lineman waving, a phone buzzing. You are also tired. Fatigue, stress and work overload make pilots fixate on one item and lose the bigger picture, and many accidents start with a distraction that began as a minor problem [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]].

bullets: Task management: once information outruns your capacity, extra items get ignored or push out more important ones [[24:51|AFH 2-14]].
Do high-workload tasks before you taxi or while stopped. Many errors happen when a pilot is off frequency or heads down [[7:6|AC 91-73B 7d(3) NOTE]].
Phones: AC 91-73B discourages cell phones and other devices during taxi and asks that everyone turn them off [[7:5|AC 91-73B 7b(2)(j)]].
Part 135 makes taxi a critical phase of flight, with only safety duties and no distracting activities [[6:33|14 CFR 135.100(a)-(c)]].

head: Distraction
Mitigation (application)
rows: Passenger asks a question during the exit
'Hold that thought until we stop'
Lineman signals while you are mid-checklist
Stop the airplane, then finish the checklist
Phone or text arrives at shutdown
Finish securing first
You are interrupted during the checklist
Restart that section from the top

callout.text: Pilots who stop taking checklists seriously drift into relying on memory alone [[24:36|AFH 1-15]]. The end of a long day is when that drift shows.

check.q: What does AC 91-73B say about nonessential communications and actions after landing?
check.a: Do not start them until you are clear of all runways [[7:7|AC 91-73B 7d(13)]].

head: Error
Fix
rows: Accepting a last-minute high-speed turnoff
Accept only if you understand it and can comply safely [[1:369|PHAK 14-35]]
Stopping with the tail still over the hold markings
Taxi until the whole airplane is past them [[7:7|AC 91-73B 7d(11)]]
Moving levers on the rollout in a retractable
Clear the runway, stop, positively identify each control [[24:248|AFH 12-17]]
Parking behind a running turboprop or jet
Pick a spot clear of blast, into the wind if possible [[24:60|AFH 2-23]]
Skipping the magneto grounding check
Check it at idle on every shutdown [[24:60|AFH 2-23]]
Passengers walking into the propeller area
Brief and lead them aft after the propeller stops [[24:54|AFH 2-17]]
Watching fueling from the office
Get passengers out and watch the grade, quantity and caps [[24:51|AFH 2-14]]
A vague or missing squawk
Write what, when and conditions in the discrepancy record [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]]
Chains pulled tight, no control lock
Slack in chains, controls secured, locks in place [[24:60|AFH 2-23]]

check.q: What is the fix for a pilot who moves levers during the rollout in a retractable-gear airplane?
check.a: Finish the roll, clear the runway, stop, and positively identify the proper controls before moving them [[24:248|AFH 12-17]] [[24:59|AFH 2-22]].

scenario.title: Dusk arrival on a photo job
scenario.setup: You are a new commercial pilot flying a retractable-gear single for an aerial photo company (a Part 91 job). You land at dusk at a busy towered regional airport you have never visited, with a photographer and her assistant aboard. Tomorrow morning you fly them home in daylight. An airline terminal with a fenced ramp sits next to the general aviation area, and the forecast calls for gusty winds overnight.

questions.q: On the rollout the tower says: 'Turn right next taxiway, hold short of Runway 27.' How do you handle the exit and the after-landing items?
questions.a: Slow to taxi speed before turning [[24:59|AFH 2-22]], exit as instructed, and stop only when the whole airplane is past the holding position markings and short of Runway 27 [[33:264|AIM 4-3-21]]. Only then run the after-landing flow, positively identifying the flap control so you do not touch the gear handle [[24:181|AFH 9-10]] [[24:248|AFH 12-17]].

questions.q: Ground clears you to 'the FBO via Alpha.' It is getting dark and you do not know the ramp. What helps you get there safely?
questions.a: Read back, keep the airport diagram up and track your progress [[7:5|AC 91-73B 7b(2)(h)]]; ask for specific instructions if unfamiliar [[33:264|AIM 4-3-21]]; follow FBO Apron destination signs [[33:169|AIM 2-3-11]]; turn strobes off if they bother others [[33:266|AIM 4-3-24]]; and watch for the boundary lines where ATC control ends [[33:159|AIM 2-3-6c]].

questions.q: The assistant starts unbuckling as you turn onto the ramp. What do you say, and when may they get out?
questions.a: Belts stay fastened while the airplane moves on the surface [[60:441|14 CFR 91.107(a)(3)]]. They get out only after the engine is shut down and the propeller has stopped, and they stay out of the propeller arc [[24:54|AFH 2-17]], moving only as you direct [[24:51|AFH 2-14]].

questions.q: A lineman drives up in a truck with a white-on-black placard and says he will top you off. What do you do?
questions.a: Stop him. White letters on black mark turbine fuel and JET-A trucks [[1:187|PHAK 7-27]] [[24:45|AFH 2-8]]. Get the right 100LL truck, have the passengers out, watch the fueling, make sure the truck is grounded before the nozzle touches the airplane [[1:189|PHAK 7-29]], and check the caps afterward [[24:51|AFH 2-14]].

questions.q: On the postflight you find the left position light out. Tomorrow's flight is in daylight. What are your options?
questions.a: Write it up [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]]. Without an MEL you may defer it under 91.213(d) if it is not required for day VFR or by the equipment list or an AD, it is deactivated (for example, circuit breaker pulled) and placarded "Inoperative," and a rated pilot or mechanic decides it is no hazard [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)]]. The PHAK uses this same daytime position light example [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]]. The owner must have it fixed or inspected at the next required inspection [[60:521|14 CFR 91.405(c)]].

questions.q: How do you leave the airplane for the night, given the wind and the airline ramp?
questions.a: Park headed into the forecast wind if the spots allow, chock, tie down (ropes cinched, chains with some slack), install the control lock, covers and security locks [[24:60|AFH 2-23]]. Brief the passengers that the airline area is a SIDA they may not enter without a badge, and use the FBO's exit [[33:173|AIM 2-3-15]] [[33:174|AIM 2-3-15]].

skills.do: Park in a suitable spot and heading, clear of other airplanes' blast, into the wind when possible, with the nosewheel straightened, while protecting nearby people and property. No numeric tolerance.
skills.practice: On every arrival say out loud why you picked the spot: blast, wind, people, exit path [[24:60|AFH 2-23]].

skills.do: Use the POH after-landing, shutdown and securing checklists at the right times, starting only when stopped clear of the runway. No numeric tolerance.
skills.practice: Fly the flow, then read the checklist item by item to confirm, every flight [[24:36|AFH 1-15]] [[24:59|AFH 2-22]].

skills.do: Walk around the airplane after flight, find leaks, stains, tire and propeller damage, check oil and fuel, and write down any discrepancy or servicing need. No numeric tolerance.
skills.practice: After each lesson write one practice squawk, even if it only says 'no discrepancies,' and have your CFI critique it [[24:60|AFH 2-23]] [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]].

skills.do: Secure the airplane: chocks, tie-downs or hangar, control lock, covers and security locks as the airplane and weather need. No numeric tolerance.
skills.practice: Practice tying down with both ropes and chains, and installing your airplane's gust lock and covers, until you can do it without the checklist and then confirm with it [[24:60|AFH 2-23]].

quiz.q: Compared with the private ACS After Landing, Parking, and Securing Task, the commercial version:
options: Adds a taxi speed tolerance of a few knots on the ramp
Has the same elements and no numeric tolerances
Adds a fueling skill element with a fuel-grade tolerance
Drops the postflight inspection and keeps only the securing steps
quiz.why: Both list the same K, R and S elements and neither has numeric tolerances (ACS PA.XII.A and CA.XI.A).

quiz.q: A marshaller draws the flat of his hand across his throat. What does he want?
options: Insert chocks
Cut engines
Slow down
Stop immediately and hold the brakes
quiz.why: That is the cut engines signal in the AIM figures [[33:273|AIM 4-3-26]].

quiz.q: Taxiing in, you cross a dashed yellow line and then a solid yellow line beside it. You have just:
options: Entered a runway safety area by the runway
Crossed an ILS critical area boundary line
Left the movement area for the nonmovement area
Entered a SIDA, where airline passengers board
quiz.why: Nonmovement area boundary markings are two yellow lines, dashed on the movement side and solid on the nonmovement side [[33:159|AIM 2-3-6c]].

quiz.q: A fuel truck is used to refuel your airplane. When should the truck be grounded?
options: After the fuel cap is removed, so the fuel can flow freely
After fueling, before the nozzle is removed from the tank
Only if you wear nylon clothing that could build static
Before the fuel nozzle contacts the aircraft
quiz.why: A fuel truck should be grounded before the nozzle contacts the aircraft, and the nozzle stays bonded throughout fueling [[1:189|PHAK 7-29]].

quiz.q: An inoperative item was deferred under 14 CFR 91.213(d). When must the owner have it repaired, replaced, removed or inspected?
options: At the next required inspection
Before the next flight for hire
Within 10 flight hours of the deferral
Within 30 days of the deferral
quiz.why: The owner or operator must have it repaired, replaced, removed or inspected at the next required inspection [[60:521|14 CFR 91.405(c)]].

quiz.q: The AFH says fuel stains that look old:
options: Still warrant further investigation
Can be ignored if the fuel gauges agree
Matter only on wet-wing airplanes
Are normal after topping off
quiz.why: Fuel stains anywhere on the wing or near a tank warrant investigation no matter how old they look; they are a sign of probable leakage [[24:46|AFH 2-9]].

quiz.q: In an airplane with no door between cockpit and cabin, AC 91-73B suggests asking passengers to keep a sterile cockpit on arrival until:
options: You turn final, when the landing checklist begins
The airplane is safely stopped at the terminal
The airplane touches down and the wheels are on the runway
You contact ground control after leaving the runway
quiz.why: The same procedure applies on arrival, from the start of landing preparations until the aircraft is safely stopped at the terminal [[7:5|AC 91-73B 7c]].

quiz.q: You push the airplane into a crowded shared hangar for the night. According to the AFH, what else should you do?
options: Leave enough room so it cannot hit the hangar, another aircraft or a vehicle, and inspect it for damage after hangaring
Leave the parking brake set overnight in place of chocks
Skip the control lock, since the hangar blocks the wind
Drain the fuel tanks to reduce the fire risk
quiz.why: Hangaring has its own hazards: allow enough space so the airplane is free from impact with the hangar, another aircraft or a vehicle, and inspect it after hangaring. Flight controls are still secured and locks installed [[24:60|AFH 2-23]].

quiz.q: While your airplane is being fueled, a technician offers to service its oxygen system. The PHAK says:
options: Oxygen servicing is not recommended during fueling
Fine, if the fuel truck is grounded and bonded to the aircraft
Do it first, then fuel once the oxygen work is done
Only with passengers aboard to watch the servicing
quiz.why: Oxygen system servicing is not recommended during fueling or other work that could provide an ignition source [[1:200|PHAK 7-40]].

quiz.q: Requesting a published Standard Taxi Route (STR) by name tells ATC that:
options: You also want clearance across every runway on it
You have priority over other taxiing aircraft
You are fully familiar with the STR
You need progressive instructions
quiz.why: By requesting an STR a pilot acknowledges full familiarity with it. An STR is not a runway crossing clearance and gives no right of way [[33:263|AIM 4-3-20]].

final_quiz.q: You park on an FBO ramp next to a fenced airline area. Your passenger sees an open gate in the fence and wants to cut across the airline ramp to the terminal. What is correct?
options: Fine if you walk with him, since you hold a pilot certificate
Fine in daylight, when the tower can see the ramp
Stop him: a secured area is always a SIDA, entry needs authorization and displayed ID, and he could be reported to TSA and fined
Fine if he shows his driver's license to the first airline worker he meets
final_quiz.why: A Secured Area, where airline passengers board, is always a SIDA, and moving into it without authorization and displayed identification is prohibited [[33:173|AIM 2-3-15]]. People seen entering without proper ID may be reported to TSA or airport security and face civil and criminal fines; pilots should brief passengers on this [[33:174|AIM 2-3-15]]. A pilot certificate is not SIDA authorization.

final_quiz.q: You fly a Part 135 Cessna 206 for an air taxi. The landing light bulb burns out on the last leg. What is correct?
options: Replace it yourself under 43.3(g); bulbs are preventive maintenance and you hold a pilot certificate
Replace it and sign the entry with your commercial certificate number
Ignore it; landing lights are never required on a Part 135 flight
Enter it in the maintenance log; 43.3(g) does not let you do this on a 135 aircraft
final_quiz.why: Replacing landing light bulbs is preventive maintenance [[60:142|14 CFR part 43 app. A(c)(17)]], but pilot preventive maintenance under 43.3(g) excludes aircraft used under part 121, 129 or 135 [[60:130|14 CFR 43.3(g)]]. The 43.3(h) and (i) exceptions cover only approved remote-area rotorcraft items and cabin seats, stretchers and oxygen bottles, never a bulb [[60:130|14 CFR 43.3(h), (i)]]. The PIC enters irregularities in the maintenance log [[6:21|14 CFR 135.65(b)]].

final_quiz.q: After sunset you park on an unlit transient spot right next to a taxiway used for night operations. Your airplane has no other lighting. Under 14 CFR 91.209, what satisfies the rule?
options: Leaving the beacon on
Nothing; the rule applies only while moving
Putting the reflective covers on
Leaving the position lights on, or moving to a lit area or one marked by obstruction lights
final_quiz.why: From sunset to sunrise you may not park in or dangerously close to a night flight operations area unless the airplane is clearly illuminated, has lighted position lights, or is in an area marked by obstruction lights [[60:491|14 CFR 91.209(a)(2)]].

final_quiz.q: Walking to your airplane you pass behind a business jet whose beacon is off. Can you assume its engines are off?
options: Yes; the beacon program requires beacons whenever engines are running
Yes, if the pilot is visible in the seat with the door shut
No; the beacon program is voluntary, so do not rely on it alone
No, unless the chocks are in place under the wheels
final_quiz.why: The FAA encourages beacons whenever engines run, but the program is voluntary; do not rely solely on the beacon as an indication [[33:266|AIM 4-3-24]].

final_quiz.q: You fly a club airplane that four pilots flew today. On the postflight, how should you check the tires?
options: Move the airplane slightly to see the whole circumference
Look only at the side facing you as you walk up to the airplane
Check pressure only, since the pilots before you checked the tread
Skip them; the next pilot will check them on his preflight
final_quiz.why: On airplanes flown by several pilots, earlier tire history is unknown, so move the airplane a little to see the complete tire [[24:48|AFH 2-11]].

final_quiz.q: You exit onto a short connector. An adjacent parallel runway's hold short line is just ahead, and your tail is still over your landing runway's hold markings. What do you do?
options: Cross the parallel runway's hold line to clear yours
Back up onto the landing runway
Stop and immediately advise ATC
Wait silently for the next airplane to land
final_quiz.why: If an adjacent parallel runway's hold short line keeps you from clearing the landing runway, stop and advise ATC immediately [[7:7|AC 91-73B 7d(11)]]. Never enter another runway without authorization [[33:264|AIM 4-3-21]].

final_quiz.q: Still at 50 knots on the rollout, the tower says 'turn left at Charlie' and Charlie is just ahead. Best response?
options: Brake hard and make the turn at Charlie as the tower asked
Make the turn at speed, since the tower needs the runway cleared for the next arrival
Stop on the runway and wait for the tower to give a new instruction
Say 'unable Charlie' and exit at a later taxiway you can make safely
final_quiz.why: Do not accept last-minute turnoff instructions unless you clearly understand them and can safely comply [[7:7|AC 91-73B 7d(14)]] [[1:369|PHAK 14-35]]; turning at speed risks gear and tire damage [[24:59|AFH 2-22]].

final_quiz.q: You will fly a Part 135 airplane that another pilot flew last. What must you do before your flight about its maintenance log?
options: Nothing; the operator handles it
Only read the last annual entry
Sign off the open items yourself
Determine the status of each irregularity entered at the end of the preceding flight, if you do not already know
final_quiz.why: Before each flight the PIC must determine the status of each irregularity entered in the maintenance log at the end of the preceding flight [[6:21|14 CFR 135.65(b)]].

final_quiz.q: In cruise the ammeter shows a steady discharge. Which is right?
options: Defer it in flight under 91.213(d) and continue to destination
Ignore it until the annual inspection comes due
Follow the POH procedure now; write it up after landing
Pull the master and continue to destination without electrics
final_quiz.why: Maintenance deferrals are not used for in-flight discrepancies; use the AFM/POH procedures [[1:239|PHAK 9-9]]. Document it on the ground so the owner can repair it [[60:520|14 CFR 91.405(a)]].

final_quiz.q: You are just repositioning an airplane across the FBO ramp to the fuel pit, not flying. Which rule still applies?
options: None; Part 91 operating rules cover only flight, not movement on the airport surface
14 CFR 91.13(b), careless or reckless operation on the airport surface
Only airport rules set by the FBO or the airport manager
Only 14 CFR 91.209, which covers lights while parked
final_quiz.why: 91.13(b) covers operating an aircraft other than for air navigation on any part of an airport surface used for air commerce, including passenger and cargo areas [[60:436|14 CFR 91.13(b)]].

final_quiz.q: After topping off on a sloped ramp, the gauges read slightly below full. What is the best check?
options: Trust the gauges
Visually check the fuel level in each tank; slope and strut extension change capacity
Add 10 percent to the gauge reading
Taxi to level ground and read the gauges
final_quiz.why: Ramp slope and strut extension change the airplane's attitude and fuel capacity; confirm quantity by looking in each tank [[24:46|AFH 2-9]].

final_quiz.q: A TSA officer on the ramp asks to see your pilot certificate. What applies?
options: 49 CFR 1540 requires you to present it
You may refuse; only the FAA can ask to inspect it
Only if you are in a SIDA at the time
Only if you are flying for hire that day
final_quiz.why: 49 CFR 1540 requires each holder of an FAA airman or medical certificate to present it for inspection on request from TSA [[33:174|AIM 2-3-15]].

final_quiz.q: No MEL. The autopilot pitch servo has failed and you want it removed from the airplane so you can fly without it. Who must do the removal?
options: You, as a commercial pilot, since pilots may remove equipment
Certificated maintenance personnel, recorded under part 43
Any pilot, with a logbook entry describing what was removed
The owner, with no record needed in the logs
final_quiz.why: Removal always involves maintenance and must be done by certificated maintenance personnel and recorded under part 43 [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]] [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(3)]].

takeaways: The flight ends when the airplane is secured, not at touchdown.
Exit at speed you can control, get every part past the hold markings, stop, then do the checklist.
In a retractable, touch no lever until clear and stopped, and identify each control first.
Park clear of blast and into the wind; treat every propeller as live; lead passengers aft.
Watch the fueling: right grade, grounding and bonding, caps on, quantity seen with your eyes.
Write squawks the next pilot and the mechanic can act on; know 91.7, 91.405, 91.213(d), 43.3(g) and 135.65.
Secure for the weather and the airport's security rules before you leave.
cfi_notes: The commercial and private ACS elements for this Task are word for word the same (ACS PA.XII.A and CA.XI.A). Raise the bar through scenario questions: for-hire passengers, Part 135 logs, fueling at strange fields, night parking.

Sources disagree: PHAK 9-12 says certificated pilots, excluding student, sport and recreational pilots, may do preventive maintenance [[1:242|PHAK 9-12]]. Current 14 CFR 43.3(g) lets any holder of a part 61 pilot certificate do it on an aircraft he or she owns or operates, except sport pilots, who are limited to light-sport category aircraft [[60:130|14 CFR 43.3(g)]]. Teach the regulation, then add 43.7(f): approving the return to service takes at least a private pilot certificate [[60:132|14 CFR 43.7(f)]], so a student or recreational pilot cannot sign off the work.

Point out what commercial students miss: 43.3(g) does not cover aircraft used under part 121, 129 or 135 [[60:130|14 CFR 43.3(g)]]. The only carve-outs, 43.3(h) and (i), need the Part 135 operator's FAA approval, training and written authorization, and cover only listed items on rotorcraft in remote areas, or removing and reinstalling cabin seats, stretchers and (without tools) oxygen bottles in aircraft with 9 or fewer passenger seats [[60:130|14 CFR 43.3(h), (i)]]. Neither covers a bulb, so a charter pilot writes it up instead of changing it.

AFH Figure 2-13's note says the emergency stop signal is used for all stops at night [[24:52|AFH 2-15]]; the AIM night figure says wands use the same hand movements as by day [[33:273|AIM 4-3-26]]. They fit together, but students should expect variations: the AFH also says local signal sets differ and what matters is an agreed set [[24:52|AFH 2-15]].
AC 91-73B dates from 2012. Its single-pilot taxi habits still match the current AIM 4-3-21, but some links and examples in it are old; use it for technique, the AIM for procedure.
Examiners often ask applicants to explain the reason for each shutdown item, especially the magneto grounding check [[24:53|AFH 2-16]]. Have students teach the shutdown back to you.

Retractable-gear airplanes make the 'nothing until clear and stopped' rule a gear-up-on-the-ground prevention rule [[24:248|AFH 12-17]]. Make the student touch and name the flap handle before moving it.
Use the 121.5 MHz check before shutdown as a habit, especially after a firm landing [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4]]; it is not on most POH checklists.
Bring a real squawk sheet or maintenance log page from the school or a Part 135 operator to class and have students write entries for the scenario discrepancies.
gaps: Exact after-landing and shutdown items, rpm values, turbocharger spool-down times and the reason for the avionics and alternator order come from the POH/AFM; the AFH list is generic [[24:60|AFH 2-23]].

The sources give no tie-down technique (knots, rope type, tie-down spacing) and no wind speed at which to add more tie-downs or move to a hangar. Use the POH ground handling section [[1:235|PHAK 9-5]] and CFI technique.
Airport-specific security procedures (gate codes, badge rules, escort policies, TSA programs for operators) are set by each airport and operator; the sources go no further than AIM 2-3-15.
No source gives a standard format for a squawk or discrepancy entry by a pilot; a Part 135 operator puts its maintenance log procedure in its manual [[6:21|14 CFR 135.65(d)]].
The sources do not say how to fight a fuel fire on the ramp or which extinguisher type fits which fire in a light airplane; that is airport, FBO and POH training.

activities.title: Postflight: what to look at here
activities.intro: Drag each check to the part of the airplane it belongs to.

pins.label: Nicks, cracks or erosion on the blade
Obstructions in the cooling air inlet
Oil or fuel streaks on the cowling
Cracked lens or failed bulb to write up

activities.title: Read the destination sign
activities.intro: Tap a sign legend, then what it means.

pairs.r: Parking for based aircraft, such as tie-downs
Where aircraft get fuel or related services
Gates where aircraft load passengers and cargo

activities.title: True or false: ramp, blast and propellers
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: Exhaust blast or rotor downwash from a powerful aircraft can make a light airplane uncontrollable.
With the magneto switch OFF and the propeller stopped, the engine cannot fire.
cards.why: False. A faulty switch can be OFF and still let current flow in the magneto circuit, so the engine could start [[24:53|AFH 2-16]].

cards.s: If chocks must be pulled with an engine running, approach them from the front so the pilot can see you.
cards.why: False. Set the throttle to idle and approach the chocks only from behind the propeller, never from the front or side [[24:54|AFH 2-17]].

cards.s: At night a marshaller with lighted wands uses the same hand movements as in daylight.
Unless you park in a supervised area, you should pick a spot and heading where other airplanes' blast will not strike yours unnecessarily.
Keep the strobes on while taxiing onto a busy ramp at night so ground crews can see you.
cards.why: False. Strobes should not be on during taxi if they adversely affect the vision of other pilots or ground personnel [[33:266|AIM 4-3-24]].

activities.title: Fueling from a drum: put it in order
activities.intro: Use the arrows to put the steps in order, then tap Check.
steps: Place the drum near a grounding post
Connect the drum or nozzle to the aircraft
Fuel through a bonded nozzle, filter and funnel
Replace the cap, then disconnect in reverse order

activities.title: Which rule says it?
activities.intro: Tap a duty, then tap the rule it comes from.

items.t: The PIC decides whether the airplane is in condition for safe flight
The PIC discontinues the flight when an unairworthy structural condition occurs
The owner has discrepancies repaired between required inspections
The owner makes sure maintenance records show the return to service
An inoperative item is deactivated and placarded "Inoperative" to fly without an MEL
The inoperative item may not be part of the VFR-day type certification equipment
A part 61 pilot other than a sport pilot may do preventive maintenance on an aircraft he or she owns or operates
With FAA approval of the Part 135 operator, a trained pilot may remove and reinstall cabin seats in a small aircraft

activities.title: Servicing and paperwork numbers
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: The lineman tops off your tanks with 34 gallons of 100LL. Avgas weighs 6 pounds per gallon. How much weight did you add for tomorrow's weight and balance?
The airplane will sit for a week. Its tanks hold 52 gallons, and you confirm 17 gallons by looking in the tanks. How many gallons should the lineman add to fill them and limit condensation?
items.why: If the airplane will be inactive, filling the tanks prevents water condensation [[24:60|AFH 2-23]]. 52 - 17 = 35 gallons.

items.q: You land weighing 2,740 lb with two passengers aboard (175 lb and 150 lb). They get off, and the lineman adds 30 gallons of 100LL for your solo flight tomorrow. With you still aboard, what does the airplane weigh now?

Your ELT went off by accident for 25 minutes after a hard landing last week, and for 40 minutes today before you caught it on 121.5 MHz. How many cumulative minutes has it transmitted? (More than 60 means the battery must be replaced.)
items.why: 25 + 40 = 65 minutes, which is more than 1 cumulative hour, so the battery must be replaced (or recharged) [[60:489|14 CFR 91.207(c)(1)]] [[1:239|PHAK 9-9]]. Report the false activations to the nearest air traffic facility [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4]].

activities.title: Saturday ferry flight, one decision at a time
activities.intro: You are a commercial pilot delivering a four-seat retractable single for its owner, who rides along. You land at a non-towered airport with two intersecting runways. The FBO is on the far side of the crossing runway. It is late afternoon and you are tired.

steps.s: Your taxiway to the FBO crosses Runway 4. Nobody has said anything on the CTAF for five minutes.
options: Cross right away; five minutes of quiet on the CTAF means nobody is on the approach or the runway
Cross with the landing light on so that any arriving traffic can see you
Ask UNICOM for a crossing clearance and cross when they say it is clear
Stop, listen on the CTAF, scan the full runway and its approach and departure paths, then cross
steps.why: Not all aircraft are radio-equipped. Listen on the CTAF and scan the full length of the runway, including approach and departure paths, before crossing [[7:7|AC 91-73B 7d(12)]]. UNICOM cannot clear you across a runway.

steps.s: A lineman marshals you into a tie-down. You stop with the nosewheel still turned about 20 degrees.
options: Shut down with the wheel turned; a lineman with a towbar can straighten it later when the airplane is moved
Let the airplane roll straight ahead a little to straighten the nosewheel, then stop
Pivot on one brake to center the nosewheel before the engine is stopped
Have the owner push the tail sideways until the nosewheel centers
steps.why: After stopping in the desired direction, let the airplane roll straight ahead enough to straighten the nosewheel [[24:60|AFH 2-23]].

steps.s: Before shutdown you tune 121.5 MHz and hear an emergency tone. Your landing was firm.
options: Ignore it; it is probably another airplane
Shut down quickly so the battery saves the ELT
Turn off your ELT to see if it is the source; if it was activated, notify the nearest ATC facility and have maintenance check it before re-arming
Leave it on so search and rescue can test it
steps.why: Hard landings can activate ELTs. If you hear a signal, turn off your ELT to see if it is transmitting; if it was activated, maintenance might be needed before it is re-armed, and you should notify the nearest air traffic facility [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4]].

steps.s: The lineman arrives to top off the tanks while the owner stays in the back seat to finish a phone call.
options: Ask him to get out, and watch the fueling yourself for grade, quantity and caps
Let him stay in the back seat; he owns the airplane and knows exactly how much fuel it takes
Go inside to pay for the fuel while the lineman fuels the airplane
Ask the owner to keep an eye on the fueling from his seat and tell you of any problem
steps.why: During refueling, take all passengers out of the airplane and witness the fueling yourself to make sure the right fuel and quantity go in and the caps and cowls are secured afterward [[24:51|AFH 2-14]].

steps.s: On the postflight you find fresh oil streaks running from the propeller hub toward the blade tips. The owner wants to fly home tomorrow.
options: Write it up and do not fly until maintenance has looked at it
Wipe it off and check again tomorrow morning before the flight home
Defer it under 91.213(d) with a placard and fly home
Fly home low and slow so any further leak can be handled
steps.why: On a controllable-pitch propeller, oil streaking from the hub toward the tips points to a hub leak [[24:49|AFH 2-12]]. The PIC must judge the airplane's condition [[60:436|14 CFR 91.7]] and the owner must have discrepancies repaired [[60:520|14 CFR 91.405(a)]]. A 91.213(d) deferral covers inoperative instruments and equipment, not a leaking propeller.
